docs.title: Cohere CEO and ex-Google researcher Aidan Gomez on how AI makes money
docs.content:
Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez on how generative AI will bring more profit to companies

Aidan Gomez is the CEO and co-founder of Cohere and he's been at the center of generative AI since its early days. He was an intern at Google in 2017, when he helped write the foundational paper that conceptualized the transformer - the tech that makes generative AI possible. Now he's focused on building generative AI models for companies instead of consumers. CNBC's Steve Kovach sat down with Gomez to talk about the burgeoning tech and specific ways his models will boost profits for companies.

**Aidan Gomez** is a British-Canadian[[1]](#cite_note-1) computer scientist working in the field of [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), with a focus on [natural language processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing").[[2]](#cite_note-2) He is the co-founder and CEO of the technology company [Cohere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohere "Cohere").[[3]](#cite_note-time100ai-3)[[4]](#cite_note-valued-4)

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aidan_Gomez&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Gomez grew up in [Brighton, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton,_Ontario "Brighton, Ontario").[[5]](#cite_note-5) He graduated from the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto") with a bachelor's degree in computer science and mathematics.[[6]](#cite_note-impact-6) He was pursuing a PhD in computer science from the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford").[[7]](#cite_note-intelligence-7) He paused his studies to launch Cohere. He was granted the PhD in 2024.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aidan_Gomez&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 2017, as a 20 year-old intern at [Google Brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Brain "Google Brain"), Gomez was one of eight authors of the research paper "[Attention Is All You Need](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_Is_All_You_Need "Attention Is All You Need")",[[9]](#cite_note-9) which is credited with changing the AI industry and helping lead to the creation of [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT").[[3]](#cite_note-time100ai-3)[[4]](#cite_note-valued-4)[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) The paper proposed a novel deep learning architecture called the [transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_(machine_learning_model) "Transformer (machine learning model)"), that enables machine learning models to analyze large amounts of data for patterns, and then use those patterns to make predictions while leveraging GPU parallelization. It has been commonly adopted for training [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") and in the development of [generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI").[[3]](#cite_note-time100ai-3)[[12]](#cite_note-trailblazers-12)

In the same year, Gomez founded FOR.ai,[[7]](#cite_note-intelligence-7) a program to help researchers learn machine learning techniques in a collaborative format. An outgrowth of this project was Cohere For AI (now Cohere Labs), which released Aya, an open-source multilingual [LLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model").[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-Snyder24-15)

As a PhD student, Gomez worked as a machine learning researcher at [Google Brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Brain "Google Brain").[[7]](#cite_note-intelligence-7) At that time, he co-authored the paper "One Model to Learn Them All" about [multi-task learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-task_learning "Multi-task learning") by a single [neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network "Neural network").[[6]](#cite_note-impact-6)

In 2019, Gomez left Google Brain to launch Cohere, an enterprise-focused company that helps businesses implement AI into chatbots, search engines, and other products.[[3]](#cite_note-time100ai-3)[[4]](#cite_note-valued-4)[[16]](#cite_note-16) As of Sept 2025, Cohere has raised about US$1.6 billion at valuation north of $7 billion, as Gomez leads the company as its CEO.[[17]](#cite_note-17) In April 2026, Cohere acquired [Aleph Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleph_Alpha "Aleph Alpha"), a German AI company, creating a combined company with a $20 billion valuation.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Gomez was named to the 2023 [*Time* 100/AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") list of the most influential people in the field of artificial intelligence.[[3]](#cite_note-time100ai-3) He and his fellow Cohere founders Ivan Zhang and [Nick Frosst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Frosst "Nick Frosst") were named number 1 on 2023 *[Maclean's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maclean's "Maclean's")* AI Trailblazers Power List.[[12]](#cite_note-trailblazers-12)

In April 2025, Gomez was elected to the board of [Rivian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivian "Rivian").[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)

## Views on AI

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aidan_Gomez&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Views on AI")]

Gomez has stated that warnings regarding the [existential risk from artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_intelligence "Existential risk from artificial intelligence") are overblown, and that real risks involve the automated spread of misinformation on social media.[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) He said that the United States would win the [AI arms race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competition_in_artificial_intelligence "Competition in artificial intelligence") over China.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

# Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez on what to expect from 'AI 2.0'

Lakshmi Varanasi

2 min read

* Companies will soon focus on customizing AI solutions for specific needs, Cohere's CEO says.
* AI 2.0 will "help fundamentally transform how businesses operate," he wrote.
* Major AI companies like OpenAI are also releasing tools for customization.

If this was the year companies adopted AI to stay competitive, next year will likely be about customizing AI solutions for their specific needs.

"The next phase of development will move beyond generic LLMs towards tuned and highly optimized end-to-end solutions that address the specific objectives of a business," Aidan Gomez, the [CEO and cofounder of Cohere](https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-rival-says-model-cheaper-more-accurate-than-gpt-4-2024-5?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoo.com), an AI company building technology for enterprises, wrote in a post on LinkedIn last week.

"AI 2.0," as he calls it, will "accelerate adoption, value creation, and will help fundamentally transform how businesses operate." He added: "Every company will be an AI company."

Cohere has partnered with major companies, including software company Oracle and IT company Fujitsu, to develop customized business solutions.

"With Oracle, we've built customized technology and tailored our AI models to power dozens (soon, hundreds) of production AI features across Netsuite and Fusion Apps," he wrote. For Fujitsu, Cohere built a model called Takane that's "specifically designed to excel in Japanese."

Last June, [Cohere partnered](https://www.businessinsider.com/mckinsey-ai-consulting-focus-future-2024-6?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoo.com) with global management consulting firm McKinsey & Company to develop customized generative AI solutions for the firm's clients. The work is helping the startup "build trust" among more organizations, Gomez previously told Business Insider.

To meet the specific needs of so many clients, Gomez has advocated for [smaller, more efficient AI models](https://www.businessinsider.com/cohere-ceo-aiden-gomez-ai-race-meta-openai-microsoft-2024-8?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoo.com). He says they are more cost-effective than building large language models, and they give smaller startups a chance to compete with more established AI companies.

But it might be only a matter of time before the biggest companies capitalize on the customization trend, too.

OpenAI previewed an advancement during its ["Shipmas" campaign](https://www.businessinsider.com/everything-openai-released-12-days-of-shipmas-sora-o1-2024-12?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoo.com) that allows users to fine-tune o1 — their latest and most advanced AI model, on their own datasets. So, users can now leverage OpenAI's reinforcement-learning algorithms to customize their own models.

The technology will be available to the public next year, but OpenAI has already partnered with companies like Thomson Reuters to develop specialized legal tools and researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to build computational models for identifying genetic diseases.

Cohere did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

Cohere, a leading company in the artificial intelligence sector, offers a wide range of salaries depending on job role, location, and experience.

‍

This article provides a detailed overview of compensation at Cohere, including salary ranges for various positions, geographic differences, and additional benefits such as equity and bonuses.

‍

### Salary Ranges Across Roles at Cohere

#### General Salary Overview

* Average annual pay for Cohere employees in the United States is approximately $69,409.
* The majority of salaries fall between $45,000 (25th percentile) and $85,000 (75th percentile), with top earners reaching up to $116,500 (90th percentile).
* Some sources report a broader range, with total compensation spanning from $125,000 (25th percentile) to $696,802 (90th percentile). This reflects higher-paying technical and leadership roles.

‍

#### Remote and Part-Time Positions

* Remote employees at Cohere typically earn between $30,000 and $60,000, with a median base pay of $57,000.
* Part-time roles such as AI Data Trainer (across various languages and tasks) generally offer $60,000 per year in Canada.
* Content moderation roles may start at $30,000.

‍

#### Technical and Engineering Roles

* Software Engineers in Canada receive a median total compensation of $152,000 per year. Packages range from CA$144,000 to CA$213,000+.
* Technical Program Managers in Canada have reported total compensation starting at CA$116,104.
* Solution Architects in the United States can earn up to $398,483 annually.

‍

### Factors Influencing Compensation

#### Experience and Skill Level

Salaries at Cohere vary significantly based on experience, skill set, and job function.

‍

Senior technical roles and specialized positions command higher compensation. Entry-level and part-time roles are at the lower end of the spectrum.

‍

#### Geographic Location

Compensation can differ by country and region.

‍

For example, Canadian roles such as AI Data Trainers are consistently listed at $60,000 per year. U.S. roles show a broader range due to market differences and cost of living adjustments.

‍

Global roles, local pay: salaries shaped by region and market.

‍

#### Additional Compensation: Equity and Bonuses

Cohere offers stock/equity grants to many employees. These typically follow a four-year vesting schedule: 25% vests each year, with monthly vesting after the first year.

‍

Additional pay may include bonuses, commission, profit sharing, and tips, depending on the role and performance.

‍

### Comparing Cohere’s Compensation to Industry Standards

Cohere’s pay for technical roles is competitive with other leading AI and tech companies, especially when factoring in total compensation (base salary plus equity and bonuses).

‍

Entry-level and part-time roles, particularly in [data annotation and moderation](https://www.nahc.io/blog/how-hong-kongs-talent-market-is-adapting-to-remote-work-trends), are in line with remote work standards. However, they may be lower than full-time technical positions.

‍

### What to Expect When Negotiating Your Offer

When considering a position at Cohere, candidates should review the [specific salary range for their role and location](https://www.nahc.io/salary-comparison).

‍

It is important to ask about equity, bonuses, and other benefits that may significantly increase total compensation.

‍

Candidates should also consider the [vesting schedule for stock options](https://www.nahc.io/blog/how-to-use-carta-to-optimize-equity-and-compensation-structure-for-hong-kong-startups), as this can impact long-term earnings.

‍

Benchmarking offers against industry data ensures competitiveness, especially for technical and leadership roles.

Teamwork and data drive competitive job offers.

‍

### Navigating Career Growth and Compensation at Cohere

[Cohere’s wide salary range](https://www.nahc.io/salary-benchmark) reflects its diverse set of roles, from part-time remote data trainers to high-level engineers and architects.

‍

Employees have opportunities for advancement, with compensation increasing alongside experience, responsibility, and performance.

‍

For those in technical roles, [equity and bonuses can form a substantial part of total compensation](https://www.nahc.io/salary). This makes Cohere an attractive employer in the AI sector.

About

# Where enterprise AI meets real-world purpose

Cohere builds foundational models and AI solutions that help teams turn everyday effort into extraordinary impact.

Our Mission

##### We believe AI’s highest purpose is to enhance human wellbeing. We’re committed to realizing that potential by empowering businesses to scale innovation, boost productivity, and drive progress that reaches everyone.

![Image 28: Image for Aesthetics Purposes](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/rjtqmwfu/web3-prod/fc9d89a21a12957acd79906436fba5d7be89322c-1513x1619.png?auto=format&fit=max&q=80&w=1513)

Our story

### From Toronto startup to enterprise AI

2019

#### Foundations

Cohere was founded in 2019 in Toronto with a bold vision: to do whatever it takes to scale intelligence to serve humanity.

Since then, we’ve remained focused on building enterprise AI that enhances human judgment, accelerates execution, and extends what individuals and teams can achieve on their own.

![Image 30: Featured Image](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/rjtqmwfu/web3-prod/4fe9ec3304c8f3c156c96da3e70874d94d23d566-1244x991.png?auto=format&fit=max&q=80&w=1244)

2021 – 2024

#### Early growth

Between 2021 and 2024, we secured four major funding rounds (Series A through D), raising nearly $1 billion.

This support has enabled us to scale our teams, expand globally, and continually develop cutting-edge models that power practical AI applications for the world’s leading enterprises.

![Image 32](https://cohere.com/pause.svg)

![Image 33](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/rjtqmwfu/web3-prod/2d42f2ca71196197ecae94c8f2027fd55d08a6b7-611x271.gif?auto=format&fit=max&q=80&w=611)

2022

#### Research focus

In 2022, we launched Cohere Labs, our open science initiative for solving complex machine learning problems.

Today, Cohere Labs has 4,500+ community members and has published over 100 research papers.

[Learn more](https://cohere.com/research)

![Image 34: Featured Image](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/rjtqmwfu/web3-prod/bd0094095a52f522311301f99a29c627175ec599-1240x960.png?auto=format&fit=max&q=80&w=1240)

2025 – present

#### Agentic AI for the enterprise

In 2025, we launched North, our turnkey AI platform for workplace productivity.

North’s agentic capabilities and advanced retrieval allow teams to automate routine tasks, accelerate complex workflows, and surface insights securely grounded in enterprise data.

[Learn more](https://cohere.com/north)

![Image 36](https://cohere.com/pause.svg)

### The News

There is a right and a wrong side of the AI bubble, and Cohere is on "the right side" of it, CEO Aidan Gomez told reporters at a press event Friday. The bold statement contrasts Google CEO Sundar Pichai's [recent warning](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwy7vrd8k4eo) that "no company is going to be immune, including us," if there is a burst. Cohere, which makes AI software for businesses, isn't the flashiest AI company — it hasn't achieved record-breaking funding rounds, announced massive data-center infrastructure projects, or participated in the [circular funding](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/circular-investment-deals-major-ai-104520350.html) propping up the AI heavyweights. And that's its advantage, Gomez said: "Cohere hasn't participated in a lot of the things stoking those fears."

"What are the assumptions you're making to drive your targets on that [infrastructure] buildout, and how far out are you building for?" he said. "Where you stand on that determines if you're on the right or wrong side of a potential correction."

### Know More

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei [took](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/03/business/dealbook/anthropic-dario-amodei-ai-risks.html) a similar stance this week, saying, "It's genuine uncertainty and a genuine dilemma, which we as a company try to manage as responsibly as we can." While Gomez argues Cohere could be one of the few companies to survive the worst-case scenario, taking smaller swings also means it could see less upside if there is no market correction.

# The Wealth of the Richest People in AI

June 20, 2026 • Updated October 16, 2026

[![Dan Schwarz](/authors/dan-schwarz-byline.webp)By Dan Schwarz](/#dan-schwarz)

The 60 AI billionaires, ranked by net worth and broken down by company, role, geography, age, and education.

We count 60 people whose fortunes come mainly from artificial intelligence and who are worth more than a billion dollars. For all of them, we research what is publicly known, and then produce calibrated estimates of their net worth.

We also looked into the next 88 most influential people in AI, for 148 total, to see the broader picture across a total of $377B in wealth that came primarily from AI. We calculate and visualize where that wealth comes from, showing wealth concentration, and breaking it down across US vs. China vs. Europe, frontier lab founders vs. other startup founder vs. prominent researchers vs. big tech, and other dimensions.

**Contents**

* [All 60 AI billionaires, ranked](#billionaires)
* [All 60 AI billionaires, visualized](#chart-all-57)
* [Who are the 20 richest people in AI?](#chart-20-richest)
* [How concentrated is AI wealth amongst individuals?](#chart-all-147)
* [Who leads among founders, startup founders, big tech, and researchers?](#chart-by-company)
* [Which AI billionaires are from the US, China, and Europe?](#chart-geography)
* [What kind of wealth comprises the $377B of individual AI fortunes?](#chart-by-source)
* [How are the 20 largest individual AI fortunes held?](#chart-composition)
* [How long have AI billionaires been working in AI?](#chart-tenure)
* [How old are the AI billionaires?](#chart-age)
* [Do wealthier people in AI have more degrees?](#chart-education)
* [Methodology](#methodology)

## Net worth and source of wealth of all AI billionaires

*Estimated personal net worth as of October 16, 2026. The figure is our median estimate; the range is the 80% confidence interval. Pure tech-company chiefs whose wealth is incidental to AI (Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, all richer than anyone here) are left out.*

| # | Name | Net worth | Who they are | Basis for the estimate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Liang Wenfeng | **$44B** ($36B–$56B) | Founder of DeepSeek and hedge fund High-Flyer | Liang's $43.5B median rests on a roughly 78 to 82% controlling stake in DeepSeek, whose first outside round closed in June 2026 at $52B to $59B, plus an estimated $2B to $5B from his majority-owned hedge fund High-Flyer. It sits between Bloomberg's $37.9B, which excludes High-Flyer profits, and Forbes's roughly $46B, which appears to reflect a second round at about $74.7B that had not formally closed by October 16. Sources: [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/wenfeng-liang/) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/liang-wenfeng/) |
| 2 | Greg Brockman | **$26B** ($23B–$38B) | Co-founder and president of OpenAI | Brockman's $25.6B median tracks Forbes and Bloomberg, both near $25.5B, consistent with a 2.5 to 3% OpenAI stake at the $852B valuation set in March 2026 and reconfirmed by an August 2026 employee tender, plus Stripe shares worth over $471M. His sworn May 2026 testimony that the stake was worth nearly $30B (about 3.5%) and unclosed talks at roughly $1.4 trillion drive the $38B high end. Sources: [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/greg-brockman/) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/greg-brockman/) [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/openai-reportedly-completed-a-7-billion-employee-tender-offer/) |
| 3 | Chen Tianshi | **$25B** ($23B–$26B) | Founder of AI chipmaker Cambricon Technologies | Chen's $24.5B median tracks the market value of his roughly 28.35% direct stake in Shanghai-listed Cambricon, about 178.1 million shares after a May 2026 capitalization issue, worth roughly $24.4B at the October 16 close of 915.0 CNY. Forbes ($24.5B) and Bloomberg ($24.6B) agree, his small economic interest in Beijing Aixi (which holds 7.27% of Cambricon) adds little, and the narrow range allows only for a possible block or illiquidity discount. Sources: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/chen-tianshi/) [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/tianshi-chen/) |
| 4 | Brett Adcock | **$23B** ($16B–$26B) | Founder and CEO of robotics startup Figure AI | Adcock's $23.4B median matches Forbes's real-time figure and combines a roughly 50% Figure AI stake, about $19.5B gross at the $39B September 2025 Series C that remains its last priced round, with an estimated 85% of Hark, worth about $5.1B after a May 2026 raise at a $6B valuation. The $15.5B low end allows for Bloomberg's lower implied 42% Figure stake plus heavy illiquidity discounts. Sources: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/brett-adcock/) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/gigizamora/2026/09/15/meet-the-34-newcomers-to-the-2026-forbes-400-list/) |
| 5 | Edwin Chen | **$16B** ($11B–$22B) | Founder of data-labeling firm Surge AI | Chen owns an estimated 75 to 82% of Surge AI, which was bootstrapped until mid-2025 and has no confirmed priced round in 2026, so the $15.5B median splits the difference between Forbes's $18.0B, which implies a roughly $24B company valuation, and Bloomberg's $13.0B, which values Surge at about 13 times its $1.2B 2024 revenue. The $21.5B high end assumes Surge holds the $30B valuation explored in 2025 funding talks. Sources: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/edwin-chen/) [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/edwin-chen/) |
| 6 | Ilya Sutskever | **$14B** ($9.5B–$19B) | OpenAI co-founder, now founder of Safe Superintelligence | Sutskever's $13.55B median sits just below Bloomberg's $13.8B and has two parts: the fully vested OpenAI stake he testified in May 2026 was worth about $7B, tied to the $852B valuation, and an estimated 21% of Safe Superintelligence at its last disclosed $32B valuation, about $6.7B. Nvidia's planned $5B investment in SSI came without a disclosed valuation, and the high end reflects unclosed OpenAI talks at $1.4 trillion. Sources: [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/ilya-sutskever/) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/aliciapark/2026/05/11/ilya-sutskever-testifies-he-holds-7-billion-openai-stake-second-new-billionaire-revealed-in-musk-altman-trial/) [Calcalist](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/qy9eg5jw4) |
| 7 | Dario Amodei | **$12B** ($7.9B–$17B) | Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic | Dario Amodei, the chief executive, holds a cofounder stake in Anthropic valued at the $965B Series H of May 2026, still the last priced mark despite unpriced IPO talk of $1.5 trillion to over $2 trillion. Bloomberg reads the stake as almost 1% ($7.98B) and Forbes as just over 1.6% ($15.5B); the $12.3B median weights the two evenly, since Anthropic's confidential S-1 draft does not disclose founder ownership. Sources: [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/dario-amodei/) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/dario-amodei/) [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/anthropics-ipo-prospectus-shows-sweeping-ai-vision-surging-costs-2026-09-28/) |
| 8 | Tom Brown | **$12B** ($7.9B–$17B) | Anthropic co-founder and research lead | Tom Brown, a research lead and the lead author on GPT-3, holds a cofounder stake in Anthropic valued at the $965B post-money of its $65B Series H in May 2026, as IPO talk of $1.5 trillion to over $2 trillion remains unpriced. Bloomberg reads the stake as slightly under 1% ($7.98B) and Forbes as about 1.6% ($15.5B, on the Forbes 400), and the $12.15B median sits near the midpoint because neither reading is confirmed. Sources: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/richardnieva/2026/05/29/anthropics-cofounders-worth/) [Eastbaytimes](https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/05/29/anthropic-co-founders-dario-amodei-worth-8-billion-each/) [Forbes](https://qz.com/anthropic-cofounders-forbes-400-debut-93-billion-091526) |
| 9 | Christopher Olah | **$12B** ($7.9B–$17B) | Anthropic co-founder leading interpretability research | Christopher Olah, who leads interpretability research, holds a cofounder stake in Anthropic valued at the $965B Series H of May 2026, as IPO talk of $1.5 trillion to over $2 trillion is unpriced. Bloomberg reads the stake as slightly under 1% (about $8B) and Forbes as just over 1.6% ($15.5B), and the $12.1B median spans the gap; he is missing from the Forbes 400 only because he is Canadian. Sources: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/christopher-olah/) [Eastbaytimes](https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/05/29/anthropic-co-founders-dario-amodei-worth-8-billion-each/) [Forbes](https://qz.com/anthropic-cofounders-forbes-400-debut-93-billion-091526) |
| 10 | Daniela Amodei | **$12B** ($7.9B–$17B) | Co-founder and president of Anthropic | Daniela Amodei, the president, holds a cofounder stake in Anthropic valued at the $965B post-money of the $65B Series H that closed on May 28, 2026; IPO valuations of $1.5 trillion to over $2 trillion floated after the October 14 investor day are unpriced. Bloomberg reads her stake as slightly under 1% ($7.98B) and Forbes as roughly 1.6% ($15.5B, on the Forbes 400), and the $12.1B median sits between them. Sources: [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/daniela-amodei/) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/richardnieva/2026/05/29/anthropics-cofounders-worth/) [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/anthropics-q3-revenue-surges-45-nearly-17-billion-2026-10-14/) |

Bloomberg reads his stake as just under 1% (near $8B) and Forbes as just over 1.6% ($15.5B); the $12.1B median sits between them, and a possible legacy stake from his years at OpenAI adds to the high end. Sources: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/jack-clark/) [Eastbaytimes](https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/05/29/anthropic-co-founders-dario-amodei-worth-8-billion-each/) [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/investors-temper-anthropic-ipo-valuation-expectations-over-revenue-growth-2026-10-15/) |

Bloomberg puts his stake at about 0.83% after Carta-based dilution adjustments ($7.98B) and Forbes at about 1.6% ($15.5B); the $12.1B median bridges the two because the S-1 draft does not disclose founder allocations. At 20 he was an intern at Google. His name is on the paper that created everything: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, every AI model on the planet. He's 28. His company is worth $20 billion Aidan Gomez. Born in 1998 in Canada. Studied computer science at the University of Toronto. At 20 he landed an internship at Google Brain. There he co-authored the paper "Attention Is All You Need." 8 authors. 2017. That paper introduced the Transformer architecture. Everything is built on it: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek. Every AI model in the world. Every chatbot. Every AI agent. All of it. Of the 8 co-authors, seven went on to found their own startups. Gomez became one of them. In 2019, at 21, he founded Cohere with Ivan Zhang and Nick Frosst. Frosst had worked with Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of neural networks and Nobel laureate. Hinton became Cohere's first advisor. The idea: AI not for consumers, but for business. Data security, customization, privacy. While OpenAI was building ChatGPT for everyone, Cohere was building AI for banks, insurers, governments. Royal Bank of Canada, Fujitsu, LG, Saab are clients. $240 million in annual revenue. Partnership with Microsoft. A contract with Saab for AI in the GlobalEye defense program. In April 2026 Cohere announced a merger with Aleph Alpha, Germany's largest AI startup. Combined valuation: $20 billion. Schwarz Group (owner of Lidl) invested $600 million. The digital ministers of Canada and Germany were both present at the announcement in Berlin. Gomez overtook Mistral. $20 billion versus $13.7 billion. The largest AI company outside the US and China. He's 28. Co-author of the paper that changed the world. CEO of a $20 billion company. And he's just getting started.

  OpenAI started with 11 founders. Three are still there. Two of the rest now work at Anthropic. Sam Altman and Greg Brockman still run it. Wojciech Zaremba stayed too, now focused on safety. That's the three. The other eight? A map of the whole industry. Andrej Karpathy is the freshest example. He left for Tesla in 2017, came back to OpenAI, left again to start an education company, and last month walked into Anthropic to work on pre-training. Durk Kingma, whose Adam optimizer is probably running in something you trained this year, got there in 2024 by way of Google. So a rival lab now employs two of the people who started OpenAI. Then there are the two founders nobody names. Pamela Vagata and Vicki Cheung were both on that 2015 team. Vagata left for Stripe and runs her own fund now. Cheung built an ML company after Lyft. Two of eleven were women, and they're the two you never hear about. So here's the part I keep chewing on. We treat benchmarks and launch dates like the scoreboard. The talent map is the quieter signal, and right now it points in every direction at once. One 2015 dinner seeded a roster that's spread across at least five labs, and some of them were built to outrun the one that hosted it. Maybe that's over-reading. People leave a ten-year-old company. Happens all the time. But when the authors of your founding mission are tuning your rival's models, "normal" starts doing a lot of work. Which of these moves looks like a real signal to you, and which is just a strong engineer taking a better offer?

Pre-IPO equity at Anthropic ($965B valuation) and OpenAI (confidential IPO filing) offers upside that Alphabet stock cannot match. # Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez says the Nvidia-backed lab still fights daily for AI chips

Cohere runs on rented capacity from Microsoft Azure and CoreWeave, with Ottawa putting $240 million into a Canadian CoreWeave site where it is anchor tenant. Its customers include RBC, TD Bank and PwC, and all of them depend on chips the company must secure itself.

![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/julian.png)

[Julian Lim](https://startupfortune.com/author/julian/)

· 4 min read · 567 reads

![Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez says the Nvidia-backed lab still fights daily for AI chips](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cohere-coreweave-aidan-gomez-1024x576.jpg)

*A lab valued at roughly $25 billion says chips are still the thing it can't take for granted. If you build on, invest in or buy from anyone outside the big three clouds, that tells you who gets capacity first.*

Aidan Gomez, the co-founder and CEO of Toronto-based Cohere, told Odaily in Tokyo this week that AI computing power is still in short supply and that his company has to compete for it every day. Bloomberg ran the same message under the headline 'Nvidia-Backed Cohere in a Fight to Secure AI Computing Power'.

Cohere doesn't own its data centers. Gomez told Odaily the company relies on cloud providers such as Microsoft Azure and the neocloud CoreWeave, and that it works with Nvidia on customized models. That's a different position from OpenAI or Anthropic, which have each signed their own very large capacity deals, and from the hyperscalers, which build for themselves first and sell what's left.

A renter negotiates against everyone else in the queue. Frankly, that's the uncomfortable part of the $25 billion number: it prices Cohere as a company that will sell a lot of software, but the software runs on hardware somebody else controls.

The Logic reported earlier that Cohere is the anchor tenant of a $725 million Canadian data center being built with CoreWeave, with Ottawa putting in $240 million through its AI Compute Challenge. The Logic reported the deal is likely to be a one-off for the federal compute program in size and structure. The facility will also sell compute to other customers, so Cohere doesn't get it to itself.

[![JPMorgan says lenders now demand proof AI firms can repay debt](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/jpmorgan-coreweave-justin-biemann-600x300.jpg)](https://startupfortune.com/jpmorgan-says-lenders-now-demand-proof-ai-firms-can-repay-debt/)

[JPMorgan says lenders now demand proof AI firms can repay debt](https://startupfortune.com/jpmorgan-says-lenders-now-demand-proof-ai-firms-can-repay-debt/)

JPMorgan strategist Justin Biemann says lenders now require proof of cash flow, not just an AI label, as CoreWeave's default-insurance costs hit record highs and neocloud bond spreads blow out. - [AI companies need strong cash flow fundamentals](https://startupfortune.com/jpmorgan-says-lenders-now-demand-proof-ai-firms-can-repay-debt/) - [lenders demand proof AI startups can repay debt](https://startupfortune.com/jpmorgan-says-lenders-now-demand-proof-ai-firms-can-repay-debt/)

## What the valuation assumes

Cohere announced on October 29 an initial close of its Series E, which targets up to C$7 billion (about US$5 billion) at a C$35.7 billion valuation, roughly US$25.5 billion. The Next Web reported that the Government of Canada has committed up to $1.14 billion, with Nvidia and the Schwarz Group among the other backers, and that the company said annual recurring revenue grew more than 165% year over year. It also said customers rose twentyfold to about 300, including Bell Canada, RBC, TD Bank and PwC. Cohere didn't disclose its revenue figure.

Part of that money is earmarked for 'computing power to train frontier models', according to the same report, and The Next Web also noted a commitment of around $1.2 billion toward compute infrastructure in Canada by 2030. Those are the right things to spend on. They're also spending that lands in the same market as every other buyer.

Here's the arithmetic that matters if you're weighing the valuation. Enterprise customers sign for models that answer fast and stay up. Growth of 165% needs more inference capacity every quarter, and Gomez is saying that capacity is something he has to chase, not something he can order and expect on time. A bank that signs with Cohere for private deployments is betting on delivery as much as on model quality.

For a founder, the lesson is blunt. Check where your vendor's compute comes from, how many contracts it holds, and what happens to your latency if it loses a bidding round. For an investor, the question isn't whether Cohere has demand. It plainly does. It's whether the company can convert demand into served workloads at the pace its valuation implies.

Neither Cohere nor Bloomberg has said how much capacity the company has contracted for the coming year, and the Odaily interview gave no figures. Without them, the gap between what Cohere can sell and what it can run remains the one number outsiders can't see.

# Canada’s Cohere targets C$7bn Series E for its sovereign AI

[by Tim Barnwell](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/author/tim-barnwell/)

30 Oct 2026

![A man with dark hair and a dark beard wearing a dark hoodie, in front of a city skyline backdrop.](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aidan_Gomez_Cohere_1200-900.jpg)

Aidan Gomez. Image: Cohere

CEO and co-founder Aidan Gomez said the funding round represents ‘the largest private capital raise in Canadian history’.

Canadian AI start-up Cohere has marked the initial close of a Series E funding round seeking up to C$7bn at a valuation of C$35.7bn.

Cohere describes itself as a leading provider of sovereign AI for regulated industries and governments, allowing organisations to “own, operate and govern their AI systems with greater control over their data, infrastructure and deployment”.

The company’s CEO and co-founder, Aidan Gomez, said the funding round “marks the largest private capital raise in Canadian history”.

The company is headquartered in Toronto, with operations in San Francisco, London, New York, Berlin, Montreal, Ottawa, Singapore, Paris, Tokyo, Seoul and the United Arab Emirates.

It has around 300 customers worldwide – including Aston Martin Aramco, Bell Canada, Fujitsu, PwC and TD Bank – and said it has seen major growth since the launch of its agentic AI platform North.

“Cohere will use the funding to advance our modelling and product roadmap, develop fully verticalised AI solutions for regulated industries and invest in long‑term compute infrastructure needed to train frontier‑level enterprise models,” said Francois Chadwick, its chief financial officer.

“We will continue to meaningfully scale across North America, EMEA and APAC to meet growing customer demand.”

According to the company, its “all-in-one” AI platform provides “maximum security, privacy and deployment flexibility across public and private clouds, on-premises environments, and fully air-gapped settings”.

In a blogpost yesterday (29 October), co-founders [Gomez, Nicholas Frosst and Ivan Zhang](https://cohere.com/blog/who-gets-to-build-the-frontier-for-ai?sanity-preview-perspective=drafts) said they would use the new funds “to build something increasingly essential in AI: a frontier company outside the US and China”.

They wrote: “Our ambition is to build frontier models that compete with the best in the world, a secure platform that lets institutions own the AI they run on, and cyber defences democracies can rely on.

“We don’t have to accept a future of AI run by just a few and we shouldn’t want one.”

Commitments to date for the funding round are led by companies of Schwarz Group, described as “one of Europe’s largest investors in AI and cloud infrastructure”.

New institutional and strategic investors include Bell Ventures, the UK’s Bullhound Capital and the Canadian government. Inovia Capital, Nvidia and Prosperity7 Ventures are returning investors.

“Canada’s investment in Cohere is an investment in choice, in security and in our ability to live our lives as we choose. Today, true sovereignty depends on our ability to build, adopt and govern AI on our own terms,” said Canadian prime minister Mark Carney.

“The bigger and faster Cohere can scale up their models and operations, the more businesses and governments can control where sensitive data is stored, how it is used and who can access it. We need this technology.”

Cohere said the Canada government’s equity investment would enable it to scale from the country – “supporting Canadian jobs and computing infrastructure while giving Canadians a stake in the company’s global success” – and make “commitments as part of the investment to support Canada’s economic vision and grow the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem”.

“The companies of Schwarz Group are proud to lead Cohere’s Series E investment at a pivotal moment for AI, where digital sovereignty has become a strategic imperative for global competitiveness,” said Christian Müller, CEO of Schwarz Digits.

“Digital sovereignty is about strategic choice, interoperability and holding the keys to our own data.

“Our partnership brings together Canadian AI leadership and trusted European infrastructure, giving customers greater choice and control over how they deploy secure AI.”

In August 2025, Cohere [raised $500m at a $6.8bn valuation](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/start-ups/cohere-joelle-pineau-ai-francois-chadwick-meta-uber-funding-e500m)  before adding another $100m in a ‘second close’ the following month.

In April of this year, it agreed to [acquire Germany’s Aleph Alpha](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/start-ups/cohere-buys-aleph-alpha-to-forge-sovereign-ai-alternative-to-us-big-tech) in a transatlantic deal aimed at giving governments and regulated industries an alternative to US tech giants.

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez is building private, sovereign enterprise AI for banks and governments, with 85% of revenue private, as it merges with Aleph Alpha

[Cohere](https://aimagazine.com/company/cohere) has no consumer chatbot and that focus on enterprise security is precisely the point of its business model.

The Toronto-based company makes 85% of its revenue from private deployments that run inside its customers’ own walls, whether hosted on their own physical servers or private cloud environments. This steadfast commitment to sovereign AI has effectively transformed what began as a Canadian research lab into a prominent Canadian-German group.

Following its agreement to merge with [Aleph Alpha](https://aimagazine.com/company/aleph-alpha) in April 2026, Cohere is reported to be raising up to US$3bn at a US$20bn valuation, which represents nearly three times its valuation from a year earlier.

[Schwarz Group](https://aimagazine.com/company/schwarz-group) owner [Lidl](https://aimagazine.com/company/lidl) has also committed €500m (US$545m) to anchor the business through its expansion.

> Organisations globally are demanding uncompromising control over their AI stack
> 
> 
> 
> Aidan Gomez, Co-Founder and CEO at Cohere

Cohere was founded in Toronto, [Canada](https://aimagazine.com/company/government-of-canada) in 2019 by [Aidan Gomez](https://aimagazine.com/executive/aidan-gomez), [Ivan Zhang](https://aimagazine.com/executive/ivan-zhang) and [Nick Frosst](https://aimagazine.com/executive/nick-frosst). Although Aidan co-wrote the seminal 2017 Transformer paper that underpins today’s large language models, the company chose early on not to compete for consumer market share.

Instead, it sells tailored models and agents to banks, governments, telecoms and industrial groups that cannot send sensitive data to a public cloud, deploying these systems wherever the customer chooses.

## Financial growth drives Aleph Alpha deal

This specialised enterprise focus has directly shaped the strong financial economics of the business over recent years. Cohere reached about US$240m in annual recurring revenue at the end of 2025, while maintaining impressive gross margins that average around 70%.

Before entering into the merger agreement, the company had raised about US$1.6bn from high-profile investors including [NVIDIA](https://aimagazine.com/company/nvidia), [AMD Ventures](https://aimagazine.com/company/amd), [Salesforce Ventures](https://aimagazine.com/company/salesforce), [Oracle](https://aimagazine.com/company/oracle) and [Cisco](https://aimagazine.com/company/cisco), reaching a valuation of US$7bn in September 2025.

Aidan, who is also the Chief Executive Officer at Cohere, says: “Organisations globally are demanding uncompromising control over their AI stack.”

The Aleph Alpha deal, formally agreed in April 2026, makes this international sovereign strategy entirely explicit.

> If critical AI runs through an external provider, you’re relying on their security as well as your own
> 
> 
> 
> Joëlle Pineau, Chief AI Officer at Cohere

Joëlle Pineau, Chief AI Officer at Cohere. Credit: Joëlle Pineau/LinkedIn

Under the terms, Cohere shareholders will own roughly 90% of the combined entity and Aleph Alpha will hold roughly 10%, with joint headquarters established in Toronto, Canada and Berlin, Germany.

To support this alliance, Aleph Alpha contributes expertise in small language models, European languages and specialised tokenisers.

Additionally, Schwarz Group’s €500m (US$545m) investment anchors a wider Series E funding round, ensuring the merged company will run its sovereign offering directly on STACKIT, the cloud platform operated by Schwarz Digits.

Cohere in Numbers

*   Valuation: Reported Series E talks of US$2bn to US$3bn at US$20bn in September 2026, up from US$7bn in September 2025 
*   Lead investor: Schwarz Group committed €500m (US$561m) to the Series E in 2026 
*   Revenue: About US$240m ARR at the end of 2025, with gross margins of around 70% 
*   Deployment: 85% of revenue from on-premise and private cloud deployments based on 2026 analysis 
*   Merger: Roughly 90% Cohere and 10% Aleph Alpha under the April 2026 agreement 
*   Funding: About US$1.6bn raised before the 2026 merger 
*   Embed 5: Launched October 2026 from US$0.08 per million tokens across more than 100 languages 

## Built for data security

The entire product lineup has been constructed specifically for the strict requirements of this sovereign market.

North, the agent platform created by Cohere, enables companies to build custom assistants over their own proprietary data, which allowed CoreWeave to completely overhaul its customer support operations within 90 days.

Meanwhile, Command models handle complex text generation, whereas Embed 5 targets high-performance search and retrieval.

Embed 5 launched in October 2026 starting from US$0.08 per million tokens across more than 100 languages, while tech giant Oracle has also launched more than 100 gen AI use cases built in partnership with Cohere.

[![Image 4: Youtube Placeholder](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/BUO7Lly6MwY/hqdefault.jpg)](https://aimagazine.com/news/cohere-sovereign-ai-the-aleph-alpha-merger-us-20bn-value)

As the company progresses, the focus shifts toward seamless operational integration and securing capital.

Although the US$20bn funding round was reported in September 2026, it has not been confirmed as closed, and the underlying merger still requires final regulatory approvals.

At the same time, Cohere faces an increasing number of rivals now pitching their own sovereign enterprise offerings.

The firm response to this competition is that true sovereignty must be engineered directly into the deployment architecture itself rather than simply tacked on as an optional hosting feature.

## Top technology partners

*   [**Schwarz Group and STACKIT**](https://aimagazine.com/company/schwarz-group)**:** The owner of Lidl and Kaufland is leading Cohere’s Series E with €500m (US$545m) of structured financing, and the merged company will run its sovereign offering on STACKIT, the cloud operated by Schwarz Digits.
*   **[Aleph Alpha](https://aimagazine.com/company/aleph-alpha):**The Heidelberg lab, with around 200 to 250 staff, brings small language models, European languages and tokenisers. Aidan calls its focus a really complementary one to Cohere’s general focus on large language models.
*   [**Government of Canada**](https://technologymagazine.com/company/government-of-canada)**:** Ottawa committed up to CA$240m (US$176m) in December 2024 for a domestic AI data centre for Cohere, the first investment under its Sovereign AI Compute Strategy and the 2026 Canada-Germany Sovereign Technology Alliance.
*   [**Fujitsu**](https://aimagazine.com/company/fujitsu)**:** Fujitsu launched its Takane large language model in partnership with Cohere, extending Cohere’s technology to Japanese enterprise customers that need secure, private deployments in their own language.
*   **[Microsoft](https://aimagazine.com/company/microsoft) and [AWS](https://aimagazine.com/company/amazon-web-services-aws):** Cohere’s Embed 5 models are generally available on Microsoft Foundry and Amazon SageMaker as well as Cohere’s own API and Model Vault, putting its retrieval models inside the major hyperscale marketplaces.

# Why is Cohere Acquiring Agentic AI Cybersecurity firm AISLE?

By[Rithula Nisha](/author/rithula-nisha)

![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/d5db7ac483634eda701d21110d712390:0942da003244e7fdf066336528d5f72c/joelle-pineau.webp)

At Cohere, Joelle is helping advance secure, sovereign AI that gives enterprises and governments full control over their systems. Credit: Cohere

Cohere’s Chief AI Officer Joelle Pineau says cybersecurity is ‘becoming the defining challenge of enterprise AI’ as Cohere plans to acquire AISLE

“In the area of agentic AI, cybersecurity is becoming the defining [challenge of enterprise AI](https://cybermagazine.com/news/the-mythos-ai-vulnerability-storm-key-ciso-takeaways),” notes Joelle Pineau, Chief AI Officer at [Cohere](https://cybermagazine.com/company/cohere) on LinkedIn.

This is why Cohere has announced a proposed agreement to acquire [AISLE](https://cybermagazine.com/company/aisle) – a cybersecurity company developing autonomous AI systems to identify and remediate previously unknown software vulnerabilities.

The proposed acquisition highlights Cohere’s continued investment in Europe, following its acquisitions of Reliant AI and Aleph Alpha.

By bringing AISLE’s technology and expertise into its ecosystem, Cohere aims to help organisations deploy AI securely while maintaining control over their data, infrastructure and governance.

“AISLE has been focused on defending the critical infrastructure of the open source ecosystem, and it’s done that better than many of the more well known efforts like Glasswing (Mythos) and Daybreak,” writes Aidan Gomez, Co-Founder and CEO at Cohere on LinkedIn.

Cohere CEO, Aidan Gomez | Credit: Getty

Aidan substantiates his claim by pointing to how AISLE found 29 new CVEs (common vulnerabilities and exposures) in curl – a widely used, open-source command-line tool and software library – in contrast to Mythos which found none.

“As part of Cohere, we’ll be continuing AISLE’s fantastic work defending OSS ([open source software](https://cybermagazine.com/news/red-hat-and-ibm-open-source-without-compromise)), but we’ll also work quickly to drive this technology into the hands of the world’s critical infrastructure companies to scan their software in a fully private, even air-gapped, capacity,” he says.

“I’m so excited to expand across Europe and scale AISLE's tech and team to strengthen the world’s defences against cyberattacks using agents.”

## Cohere acquisition of AISLE targets emerging AI security challenges

Businesses and public sector bodies face growing concerns around data protection, regulatory compliance, software vulnerabilities and the risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Cohere believes addressing these challenges requires an integrated approach that combines AI models, cybersecurity, governance and secure deployment infrastructure.

> I’m so excited to expand across Europe and scale AISLE's tech and team to strengthen the world’s defences against cyberattacks using agents
>
> Aidan Gomez, Co-Founder and CEO at Cohere

Its platform supports private cloud, on-premises and fully air-gapped environments, allowing organisations to adopt AI while retaining greater control over sensitive information.

“The organisations Cohere serves don’t just need powerful AI,” notes [Ondrej Vlcek](https://cybermagazine.com/executive/ondrej-vlcek), Co-Founder and CEO at AISLE on LinkedIn.

“They need AI they can trust with their most critical systems and put to work [defending them](https://cybermagazine.com/news/defense-halo-gtts-ai-native-reply-to-machine-speed-attacks).”

“Not even a year ago, we launched out of stealth with a bold mission of protecting democratic societies against AI-driven cyberattacks,” Ondrej recalls.

“And what a ride it has been! 2026 will be remembered as the year when AI started breaking software – but also, when AI became a must-have technology for defenders.

Ondrej Vlcek, Co-Founder and CEO at AISLE | Credit: Ondrej Vlcek/ LinkedIn

“At AISLE, we’ve built a system that repetitively outperformed Mythos and other [frontier models on cybersecurity tasks](https://cybermagazine.com/news/crowdstrike-launches-project-quiltworks-to-patch-the-ai-bugs) and shipped it to a number of leading organisations around the world.

“We began talking with Cohere this spring as part of a customer engagement, and as our teams worked together we realised it would be a natural fit to bring together our ecosystem of foundation models, sovereign systems, harnesses and applications.”

## AISLE AI security technology has identified hundreds of vulnerabilities

Founded in 2024, AISLE develops AI systems designed to discover, validate and help fix previously unknown vulnerabilities in complex production software.

Its approach combines foundation models with specialised security expertise, large-scale code analysis and automated remediation.

During its first year out of stealth, AISLE identified more than 500 previously unknown vulnerabilities assigned CVEs across over 100 codebases.

These included all 12 vulnerabilities in [OpenSSL](https://cybermagazine.com/news/ai-in-open-source-cryptography-auditor-not-author)’s January 2026 security release and 18 of the 24 CVEs in curl’s latest release, according to Cohere’s announcement.

![Youtube Placeholder](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/dKvgGaqkxzc/hqdefault.jpg)

The findings highlight the [potential of autonomous AI systems](https://cybermagazine.com/news/ai-safety-uk-lawmakers-push-for-data-centre-switch) to improve software security by identifying weaknesses that conventional approaches may miss.

Independent reviews by software maintainers also provide validation of the vulnerabilities discovered.

## Cohere Cyber to establish Prague as an AI cybersecurity hub

Under the proposed arrangement, AISLE’s three founders will take leadership positions at Cohere.

Ondrej will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, leading the newly established global cybersecurity business.

Cohere also plans a substantial long-term investment in Prague, Czech Republic expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global centre for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.

The proposed acquisition is expected to strengthen Cohere’s security offering through improved threat detection, AI agent monitoring, data protection and support for secure deployments in sensitive environments.

For European organisations, the move could offer greater access to advanced AI systems designed around data sovereignty, privacy and regulatory requirements.
